title: Pan Am Highway Blues
author: Ron Jacobs
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Panamericana_Atacama_Peru-680x510.jpg)

Photograph Source: Angelica Jacobi - [CC BY-SA
3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)

A friend of mine, long past and now hitchhiking on some eternal highway, used
to hitch the Pan American highway every January. From the first time I heard
about this road, I had always imagined it as a long road that ran from the
northern Mexican border to the tip of Argentina. My friend dispelled me of
that notion, describing it as neither a continuous road or a singular one. A
new book by Shawn William Miller titled [_Dream Road to Pan America: A Century
in Pursuit of the World 's Longest
Highway_](https://www.ucpress.edu/books/dream-road-to-pan-america/hardcover)
shatters that notion once and for all. Furthermore, it explains why such a
road will never be built and what exists instead.

Miller, who teaches history at Brigham Young University, remarks in his
introduction that “unlike most histories of colossal infrastructure (this
history) is not meant to be triumphal.” Instead, it is an examination of the
highway, the intentions of its champions in the capitalist and political
worlds, the geographic challenges of its construction and its perception by
those who have used it or happen to live near it. It’s a story that includes
human hubris, a certain kind of adventurer, an indifference to the environment
conjoined with the environment’s indifference to human attempts at its
exploitation, death, and humor. The reader is not only provided with a history
of a highway; they are also provided with history itself.

In the histories of the colonizer and the colonized, the edifices of the
colonizers (not to mention their armies and diseases) forever change the
lives, habits and even cultures of the colonized. The decades-long
construction of what is nowadays considered to be the Pan-American highway was
no different. Although the road in its numerous manifestations has never seen
the traffic like the roads people who live in global cities are accustomed to,
its presence has created a certain type of interaction between those who
travelled it and those who lived near it. Usually involving the buying and
selling of goods and services, those interactions exposed previously isolated
natives to people and phenomena they might otherwise never been aware of.
Likewise, the introduction to people and cultures unfamiliar to the travelers
on the roads traveled provided those travelers with the opportunity to
increase their understanding of humanity. Of course, like many such
interactions between the indigenous and the foreigner, not every foreigner on
the road utilized their interactions in this enlightened way. Indeed, Miller’s
anecdotes reveal a perception of the indigenous people by the interlopers as
potential hindrances and, at best, cheap labor. Miller does acknowledge that
there were exceptions to this general perception.

An interesting element of the history in _Dream Road to Pan America_ is how
much of the road’s construction and existence was the result of certain
industries in the United States. Those industries—mostly the auto and highway
industries—were considerably smaller than they are today, but as Miller’s
history moves forward in time, one is also witnessing the growing power of
those industries. When one looks at the world today, reading this history
reveals how rapidly these industries rose to the positions they now hold in
the world’s economy. After conquering the US imagination and economy, neither
industry stopped at its borders. At the least, a combination of hype,
political pressure and bribery, and a human desire for mobility combined with
a lack of concern for the environment and human and animal life brought us to
the situation we now exist in. This text is both a case study and a metaphor
for the process I have attempted to describe here.

Many readers of _Dream Road to Pan America_ will not be aware of the numerous
“races/contests” undertaken by fortune-seekers, celebrities, rich adventurers
of the leisure class and various scientists. Nor will they know of the Motor
Boys book series, most of which were written by Clarence Young (pseudonym for
Howard Garis), author of the Uncle Wiggly stories. These books, written in the
early twentieth century, were adventure stories written for boys and were
similar in format and style to other book series that began around the same
time (Tom Swift, Bobbsey Twins). The book series was not part of any
advertising package for the auto or highway industry, but the books were
popular and created an interest in both. Perhaps this is why Miller mentions
it in his chapter titled “Adventures in Roadless Road Trips,” which is about
what the chapter title says it’s about. These journeys were part adventure and
part hustle, both for funds and in terms of travel. The books of these
contests that often followed were of questionable veracity, but read by many
nonetheless. Jack Kerouac’s classic novel of the road _On the Road_ could be
considered a hopped-up manic, hipper and equally embellished example of this
kind of travel book, only without the pretense of being factual and for a very
different audience. Not just a history of the not truly existing pan American
highway, _Dream Road to Pan America_ is also a history of American highways in
general, their actual cost and their cost in other ways that we continue to
discover, both good and bad.

(_The title of this review was borrowed from the ZZ Top song of the same
name.-Ron J_.)
